paragraphs: “It’s very important that I get to my brother in time today,” Alyosha stammered.
“Yes, yes, of course! You’ve reminded me. Listen, what is an aberration?”
“What aberration?” Alyosha asked, puzzled.
“The legal kind. An aberration where everything is forgiven. Whatever you do, you’re acquitted on the spot.”
“What do you mean?”

“I’ll explain. This Katya ... Ah! She’s a charming, charming girl, only I can never work out who she is in love with. She was here a while ago and I couldn’t get a thing out of her. Especially since she now only talks to me about surface things. It’s always my health and nothing else, and she takes such a tone with me, too. I just told myself, ‘Well, so be it. I don’t care’... Oh, yes. I was talking about aberration. The doctor has come. You know a doctor has come? Of course you know—the one who finds out who’s mad. You wrote for him. No, it wasn’t you, it was Katya. It’s all Katya’s doing. Well, you see, a man can be sitting there perfectly sane and suddenly have an aberration. He can be conscious and know what he’s doing and still be in a state of aberration. And there’s no doubt that Dmitri Fyodorovitch was suffering from aberration. They discovered aberration as soon as the law courts were reformed. That’s all the good effect of the reformed law courts. The doctor has been here and questioned me about that evening, about the gold mines. ‘How did he seem then?’ he asked me. He must have been in a state of aberration. He came in shouting, ‘Money, money, three thousand! Give me three thousand!’ and then went off and committed the murder right away. ‘I don’t want to murder him,’ he said, and then he suddenly went and murdered him. That’s why they’ll acquit him: because he struggled against it and yet he murdered him.”
“But he didn’t murder him,” Alyosha broke in, rather sharply. He felt sicker and sicker with anxiety and impatience.
“Yes, I know, it was that old man Grigory who murdered him.”
“Grigory?” cried Alyosha.
“Yes, yes, it was Grigory. He lay there after Dmitri Fyodorovitch knocked him down, and then he got up, saw the door open, went in and killed Fyodor Pavlovitch.”
“But why, why?”

“Suffering from aberration. When he came to after the blow Dmitri Fyodorovitch gave him on the head, he was suffering from aberration; he went and committed the murder. As for his saying he didn’t, he very likely doesn’t remember. Only, you know, it will be better, ever so much better, if Dmitri Fyodorovitch murdered him. And that’s how it must have been, though I say it was Grigory. It certainly was Dmitri Fyodorovitch, and that’s better, ever so much better! Oh! Not better that a son should kill his father—I don’t defend that. Children ought to honor their parents, and yet it would be better if it were he, because then you’d have nothing to cry over, since he did it while unconscious—or rather while conscious, but not knowing what he was doing. Let them acquit him—that’s so humane, and it would show what a blessing the reformed law courts are. I knew nothing about it, but they say they’ve been reformed a long time. And when I heard it yesterday, I was so struck by it that I wanted to send for you at once. And if he’s acquitted, make him come straight from the law courts to dinner with me, and I’ll have a party of friends, and we’ll drink to the reformed law courts. I don’t believe he’d be dangerous. Besides, I’ll invite a great many friends, so he could always be led out if he did anything. And then he might be made a justice of the peace or something in another town, for those who have been in trouble themselves make the best judges. And besides, who isn’t suffering from aberration these days?—you, I, all of us are in a state of aberration, and there are ever so many examples of it: a man sits singing a song, suddenly something annoys him, he takes a pistol and shoots the first person he meets, and no one blames him for it. I read that recently, and all the doctors confirm it. The doctors are always confirming; they confirm anything. Why, my Lise is in a state of aberration. She made me cry again yesterday, and the day before, too, and today I suddenly realized it’s all due to aberration. Oh, Lise grieves me so! I believe she’s completely mad. Why did she send for you? Did she send for you or did you come on your own?”
“Yes, she sent for me, and I’m going to her now.” Alyosha got up resolutely.

“Oh, my dear, dear Alexey Fyodorovitch, perhaps that’s the most important thing,” Madame Hohlakov cried, suddenly bursting into tears. “God knows I trust Lise to you with all my heart, and I don’t mind her sending for you on the sly, without telling her mother. But forgive me, I can’t trust my daughter so easily to your brother Ivan Fyodorovitch, though I still think him the most chivalrous young man. But just imagine, he’s been to see Lise and I knew nothing about it!”
“How? What? When?” Alyosha was extremely surprised. He had not sat down again and listened standing.

“I’ll tell you. That’s perhaps why I asked you to come, though now I don’t know why I did ask you. Well, Ivan Fyodorovitch has been to see me twice since he came back from Moscow. The first time he came as a friend, to call on me, and the second time Katya was here and he came because he heard she was here. I didn’t expect him to come often, of course, knowing how much he has to do as it is, _vous comprenez, cette affaire et la mort terrible de votre papa_. But then I suddenly heard he’d been here again, not to see me but to see Lise. That was six days ago. He came, stayed five minutes, and left. And I didn’t hear of it until three days later, from Glafira, so it was a great shock to me. I sent for Lise at once. She laughed. ‘He thought you were asleep,’ she said, ‘and came in to me to ask after your health.’ Of course, that must be how it happened. But Lise, Lise, mercy on us, how she distresses me! Would you believe it, one night, four days ago, just after you saw her the last time and went away, she suddenly had a fit, screaming, shrieking, hysterics! Why is it I never have hysterics? Then the next day another fit, and the same on the third day, and yesterday too, and then yesterday that aberration. She suddenly screamed out, ‘I hate Ivan Fyodorovitch. I insist that you never let him into the house again.’ I was struck dumb by these amazing words, and answered, ‘On what grounds could I refuse to see such an excellent young man, a young man of such learning, too, and so unfortunate?’—for all this business is a misfortune, isn’t it? At my words she suddenly burst out laughing, and so rudely, you know. Well, I was pleased; I thought I had amused her and the fits would pass, especially as I wanted to refuse to see Ivan Fyodorovitch anyway, on account of his strange visits without my knowledge, and meant to ask him for an explanation. But early this morning Lise woke up and flew into a passion with Yulia and, would you believe it, slapped her in the face. That’s monstrous; I am always polite to my servants. And an hour later she was hugging Yulia’s feet and kissing them. She sent me a message that she wasn’t coming to me at all, and would never come and see me again, and when I dragged myself down to her, she rushed to kiss me, crying, and as she kissed me, she pushed me out of the room without saying a word, so I couldn’t find out what was the matter. Now, dear Alexey Fyodorovitch, I place all my hopes on you, and of course my whole life is in your hands. I simply beg you to go to Lise and find out everything from her, as you alone can, and come back and tell me—me, her mother, for you understand it will be the death of me, simply the death of me, if this goes on, or else I shall run away. I can’t stand any more. I have patience, but I may lose patience, and then ... then something awful will happen. Ah, dear me! At last, Pyotr Ilyitch!” cried Madame Hohlakov, beaming all over as she saw Perhotin enter the room. “You’re late, you’re late! Well, sit down, speak, put us out of our suspense. What does the counsel say? Where are you off to, Alexey Fyodorovitch?”
“To Lise.”
“Oh, yes. You won’t forget, you won’t forget what I asked you? It’s a question of life and death!”
“Of course I won’t forget, if I can ... but I’m so late,” muttered Alyosha, beating a hasty retreat.
“No, be sure, be sure to come in; don’t say ‘If I can.’ I shall die if you don’t,” Madame Hohlakov called after him, but Alyosha had already left the room.
